subject.question: What does it take to know that five pages of Swerdlow's exposition of Ptolemy's solar model are right, and what is found when every assertion on them is checked?

sources.note: printed page 22, scan page 52: the seasons and the parameters Ptolemy finds from them
printed page 22, scan page 52: al-Battānī's values as printed

subject.work: Noel Swerdlow, The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026), chapter 1, printed pages 17, 19, 20, 22 and 23
subject.edition: Famulus collection kepler-sec, document Swerdlow2026, scan pages 47, 49, 50, 52 and 53 (scan page n is printed page n − 30 in chapter 1)
subject.method: A deep reading: every assertion on the pages is isolated, quoted, formalised and checked, and the check is recorded so that another reader can run it again. Geometrical assertions are checked against astra/1 texts written from the same pages; numbers are recomputed in sexagesimal arithmetic or computed from the model.
limits: The reading covers five pages, not the chapter, and it covers what can be formalised: arithmetic, geometry, and the consistency of the page with itself.
It does not check Swerdlow's historical claims against the sources he cites, except where the arithmetic on the page or the model makes a claim testable.
The checks of the derivations test truth on samples of the parameter space and match rules as schemas; they are not formal proofs.
The modern values Swerdlow uses are taken as given where he does not state them.
The transcription is the OCR of the book's PDF; two quotations had to be written in the transcription's flattened form of a fraction.
'Misprint' is a judgement; Swerdlow's manuscript was not seen.
Ptolemy's steps are not on the page and were not compared with the Almagest; al-Battānī's maximum equation was not checked against al-Battānī's Zīj.

claims.text: Of 45 assertions, 35 are confirmed, one is a historical judgement that arithmetic cannot reach, and nine differ from recomputation.
claims.gap: The count is the report of the reading file readings/swerdlow-solar.yaml, for which the issue gives no fr: address.

claims.text: Seven of the nine discrepancies concern figures that Swerdlow reports from his sources and are facts about those sources: Ptolemy's rounded arcs of mean motion, al-Battānī's maximum equation, and Ptolemy's eccentricity and apogee.
Ptolemy's eccentricity and apogee follow from his rounded arcs of mean motion, to within what a computation with a table of chords loses, and not from the day counts of the seasons.

The sign rule for the equation of centre on page 22 names the same condition, κ̄ > 180°, in both of its clauses; the model under Ptolemy's parametrisation gives c > 0° for κ̄ < 180° and c < 0° for κ̄ > 180°.
The advance of al-Battānī's apogee is printed as 16;37°; the two longitudes on the page, 65;30° and 82;17°, differ by 16;47°.
The equivalence of the eccentric and the epicyclic form has hypotheses, R′ = R and r = e; lifting either makes the conclusion fail, and no step uses a given it does not cite.
The parallelogram argument does not cover the apsides: at κ̄ = 0° and κ̄ = 180° the points O, E, S and C lie on the apsidal line, and the derivation has three cases.

The two cases are called misprints because the arithmetic of the sentence does not come out as printed, the page image confirms the transcription, and a one-character change makes each sentence correct; Swerdlow's manuscript has not been seen.
claims.gap: Swerdlow's manuscript is not among the sources of the issue; where the slip entered is left open.

agent.summary: Deep reading of five pages of Noel Swerdlow's The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026) on Ptolemy's solar model: printed pages 17, 19, 20, 22, 23. 45 assertions are quoted, formalised and checked; 35 are confirmed, one is not checkable, nine differ from recomputation. Seven of the nine concern figures Swerdlow reports from his sources and are facts about those sources, not errors of his page; two are judged misprints of the page. The model read is Ptolemy's, the text read is Swerdlow's. The checks are not formal proofs; historical claims are not checked against the sources Swerdlow cites.
answers: Which assertions on Swerdlow's pages 17 to 23 about Ptolemy's solar model are confirmed, and which differ from recomputation?

terms.meaning: every assertion on the pages is isolated, quoted, formalised and checked, and the check is recorded so that another reader can run it again
one assertion of the reading with its locus, quotation, kind, formalisation, printed result, attribution and evidence
whether the assertion is Swerdlow's own statement or arithmetic (print) or a figure he reports from a source (reported); a discrepancy in the first is about the page, in the second about the source
confirmed, discrepancy (with the recomputed value and the difference), not checkable (with the reason) or quotation not found
for a geometrical assertion: the proposition holds over the model's parameter space, or the step of the derivation is true and licensed by its rule

do_not: Do not report the seven discrepancies in reported figures as errors of Swerdlow's page: they are facts about Ptolemy's computation and about Regiomontanus's report of al-Battānī.
Do not present the two misprints as established from the manuscript: the manuscript was not seen, and where the slip entered is left open.
Do not treat the reading as a check of Swerdlow's historical claims against the sources he cites.
Do not call the checks of the derivations formal proofs.
Do not present the missing cases at the apsides as an error of the page: it is what the page's one sentence of argument leaves to the reader.
Do not cite al-Battānī's recomputed maximum equation as 1;59,8°: that figure of the first version was truncated; it is 1;59,9°.

title: Reading Five Pages Deeply
subtitle: Swerdlow on Ptolemy's Solar Model, Checked Assertion by Assertion, with Two Misprints Found
abstract: Five pages of Noel Swerdlow's posthumous The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026) set out Ptolemy's solar model: the length of the year, the eccentric and the epicyclic form and their equivalence, the equation of centre, Ptolemy's derivation of the parameters from the seasons, and the later values of al-Battānī, az-Zarqāl and the Alfonsine Tables. We read these pages deeply. Every assertion is quoted and the quotation verified against the transcription. Every assertion is then checked as what it is: a property of the construction as a proposition of a model written in the language astra/1, a statement that something follows as a step of a derivation with its rule, a number as sexagesimal arithmetic or as a quantity computed from the model, parameters found from observations as a determination through the model. Every result is shown with the crop of the page it checks. Of 45 assertions, 35 are confirmed, one is a historical judgement that arithmetic cannot reach, and nine differ from recomputation. Seven of the nine concern figures that Swerdlow reports from his sources and are facts about those sources: Ptolemy's rounded arcs of mean motion, al-Battānī's maximum equation, and Ptolemy's eccentricity and apogee, which follow from his rounded arcs and not from the day counts of the seasons. Two concern the page itself and are misprints: the sign rule for the equation of centre names the same condition in both of its clauses, and the advance of al-Battānī's apogee is printed as 16;37° where the two longitudes on the page differ by 16;47°. The derivation of the equivalence, written out and checked step by step, shows further that the parallelogram argument does not apply at the apsides. The reading is a record that runs, every item of which points back to its paragraph.
